title: 用一台 M1 开始 AI 研究：先把问题和证据分清
description: 本科研究记录第一篇：在 M1、8GB 内存和零新增预算的条件下，先做机会扫描、核对前作，再决定值得验证的问题。
excerpt: 我想在本科期间，和 AI 助手一起走完一次研究过程：找问题、读论文、提出能被推翻的假设、运行实验，最后把结果写清楚。 手头的设备是一台 M1 MacBook Air，8GB 内存，没有额外的算力预算。目前按入门基础安排学习。这个系列先以中文技术长文为载体，记录每一步拿到了什么证据、还有什么不知道。 这篇记录到选题扫描为止。三个候选题还没有定下，研究实验尚未开…
body:
我想在本科期间，和 AI 助手一起走完一次研究过程：找问题、读论文、提出能被推翻的假设、运行实验，最后把结果写清楚。

手头的设备是一台 M1 MacBook Air，8GB 内存，没有额外的算力预算。目前按入门基础安排学习。这个系列先以中文技术长文为载体，记录每一步拿到了什么证据、还有什么不知道。

这篇记录到选题扫描为止。三个候选题还没有定下，研究实验尚未开始。【已验证：项目状态】

## 先确定什么可以做

在当前条件下，小模型、短输入和能由程序判定答案的任务，是值得优先尝试的起点。【有依据的推断】实际运行速度、内存占用和模型是否具备基本任务能力，都还要试运行才能知道。【待验证】

这意味着问题要足够具体。例如：“AI 在小程序上用自己生成的测试检查修复，结果可靠吗？”这样的任务可以先从几段短代码开始，正确与否也有机会用反例检查。

第一步仍然做了全景扫描。整理范围包括 AI、全栈与系统，以及量子计算、机器人、人机交互、开源生态、去中心化系统和芯片，共 23 个分方向。扫描主要核对了论文元数据、摘要和公开项目；精读将留在下一阶段。【已验证：资料整理范围】

从这张地图里，筛出了三个值得进一步查证的入口。

## 三个问题，以及它们已经有哪些前作

### 1. AI 自己写的测试，能证明代码修对了吗？

假设一个求最大值的程序错误地把初始值设成 0。只用正数测试，可能看不出问题；输入 `[-5, -2]` 就能暴露错误。这是人工构造的教学例子，不是模型实验结果。

我想进一步追问：在多轮修复中，程序和测试会不会一起继承某个错误理解，让自测越来越容易通过，独立检查却没有改善？【待验证】

这个大方向已有前作。Chen 等在 ACL 2025 的论文里分析了自生成测试偏差；Konstantinou 等的 2026 预印本研究了错误实现对后续测试生成的影响。【已验证：原文报告；尚未独立复现】[1][2]

因此，后续要查的是还有没有具体、重要的机制或改进空间。仅把同一个问题换到小模型上测一遍，未必形成新贡献。

### 2. 记忆记录删掉了，AI 为什么还能回答？

聊天系统可能同时保存原始记录、摘要和其他衍生信息。我要问的是：撤回某条信息后，它对回答的影响是否也消失了？【待验证】

这也有直接相关研究。AfterDeleteBench 的作者研究了源记录删除后，衍生状态仍可能支持信息恢复的情况，并提出了相应维护方法。【已验证：原文报告；尚未独立复现】[3]

继续做这个方向，需要核查混合来源、更新和删除的语义边界。先把“应该删除什么、应该保留什么”定义准确，才谈得上测量系统是否出错。

### 3. 量化让模型更快，也让任务更快完成吗？

如果低精度模型每次输出更快，却需要更多次重试，那么单次推理速度可能不足以描述完整任务的代价。【有依据的推断】我想知道，在同一任务与明确预算下，配置排名会不会因此改变。【待验证】

Abkin 等的近期预印本已经在 NVIDIA A100 环境研究了量化 Agent 的完整任务能耗。【已验证：论文研究范围】[4] 后续必须查清我们还能提供什么额外解释；换成自己的 M1，并不会自动产生创新。

## 给每条主张写清状态

这次记录会使用三个标签：

- **【已验证】**：已经核对来源、检查项目状态，或者确实有运行记录。转述论文时，会写清“作者报告”。
- **【有依据的推断】**：判断有依据，但还缺直接验证。
- **【待验证】**：研究问题、效果猜想或原创性判断，等待实验与文献检查。

这些标签需要配上范围。“论文确实存在”“作者报告了某个现象”“我成功复现了这个现象”，各自需要不同证据。

配套仓库里也做了一个很小的工具，检查文献字段、引用关系和状态标签是否填写一致。它只能帮助减少记录错误，论文内容仍需要人工核对。

## 接下来一起做什么

目前更推荐先精读自生成测试方向：例子容易用小程序展示，也方便检查反例。【有依据的推断】最终选题尚未确定。

后续每个阶段都会保留确认点。具体协作时，先看例子、预测结果，再确认对照是否公平；代码运行后保留命令与输出，一起解释结果，最后写进文章。AI 助手参与检索、编程和写作，关键路线与阶段推进由我决定。

如果实验推翻了原来的想法，就把反例和失败原因记下来。如果文献已经把问题研究清楚，就重新选题。第一篇日志先记录这些起点，后面再逐步补上真实证据。

项目资料与工具：[ai-research-notebook](https://github.com/sepfivepencer/ai-research-notebook)。

## 参考文献

1. **Xiancai Chen 等，2025，ACL 主会长文。** *Revisit Self-Debugging with Self-Generated Tests for Code Generation.* DOI: 10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.881。arXiv 号本轮未核实。[正式论文页](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.881/)
2. **Michael Konstantinou、Florian Tambon、Mike Papadakis，2026，预印本。** *On the risk of coding before testing: An empirical study on LLM-based test generation workflow.* arXiv:2607.05139。正式会议身份未核实。[arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05139)
3. **Ehsan Saleh、Roozbeh Nahavandi、Sama Salarian、Raef Bassily、Andrew Perrault，2026，预印本。** *AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents.* arXiv:2610.31366。正式会议身份未核实。[arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31366)
4. **Stephen Abkin、Aldric Yang、Alex Flesher、Nitheesh Kodarapu、Deepak Panigrahy、Aakash Tyagi、David Kebo Houngninou，2026，预印本。** *Measuring the Energy Cost of Completing Tasks with Quantized Language-Model Agents.* arXiv:2610.32417。正式会议身份未核实。[arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32417)

本文由我与 AI 助手协作整理。文献核验范围截至 2026 年 10 月 29 日，为元数据与摘要层面的扫描；目前没有原创性结论或模型实验结果。

title: Building a personal site that can outlast the trend cycle
description: A personal website should survive aesthetic shifts, new frameworks, and your own changing interests. That only happens when content structure comes first.
excerpt: The easiest way to ship a personal website is to treat it like a one-week design sprint. The easiest way to regret it is exactly the same. Most personal sites fail for one of two r…
body:
The easiest way to ship a personal website is to treat it like a one-week design sprint. The easiest way to regret it is exactly the same.

Most personal sites fail for one of two reasons. Either they are so generic that they never become useful, or they are so over-designed that they collapse the first time you want to publish a real post. In both cases the problem is not visual polish. The problem is that the site was never modeled as a publishing system.

For me, a durable personal site has to satisfy a few simple rules:

1. I should be able to publish without opening a component file.
2. Every post needs a stable URL that I can share without explanation.
3. The site needs to read well on a phone, not only on a 16-inch laptop.
4. The design should carry a point of view without competing with the writing.

That is why I prefer a Markdown-first setup for a personal blog. It keeps the content portable. If I decide to move from one framework to another a year from now, the writing survives unchanged. The content is the asset. Everything else is delivery infrastructure.

A second principle is that navigation should reflect how a person thinks, not how a template thinks. I want a home page that introduces the intent of the site, a writing index that behaves like an archive, and article pages that do not bury the actual text under decorative noise. The structure is almost boring on paper, which is exactly why it scales.

Design still matters. I like dense interfaces. I like editorial rhythm. I like a little glass, a little motion, a little atmosphere. But those choices only work when they sit on top of a system that remains legible after the novelty disappears.

That is the standard I want for this site: something personal enough to feel authored, and sturdy enough to still make sense after the next wave of fashionable interfaces moves on.

title: Designing for density without making the page feel crowded
description: Information-rich layouts are not the same thing as messy layouts. The difference is hierarchy, pacing, and the willingness to leave dead-simple components alone.
excerpt: I have always been drawn to products that show more, sooner. Dense interfaces can feel alive in a way that minimal layouts often do not. They reward curiosity. They help you build…
body:
I have always been drawn to products that show more, sooner.

Dense interfaces can feel alive in a way that minimal layouts often do not. They reward curiosity. They help you build a mental model quickly. They reduce unnecessary navigation. But density is only valuable when it increases comprehension. If it increases friction, it is just noise wearing an intelligent costume.

The most common mistake is confusing compression with hierarchy. Shrinking type, tightening margins, and stacking more boxes onto the screen does not make an interface information-rich. It makes it harder to read.

Density works when three things are true:

## 1. The page has a clear entry point

Every screen needs an obvious place to start. On a blog, that is usually the headline, summary, and the first meaningful group of posts. If the eye has no anchor, the user has to negotiate the layout before they can absorb the content.

## 2. Repetition is controlled

Repeated components should feel dependable, not decorative. When every card has a different accent treatment, every list turns into a negotiation. I would rather spend my expressive energy on the overall atmosphere than on making every individual block shout for attention.

## 3. The layout changes pace

A dense page needs intervals. A wide hero, a quiet summary block, a single featured card, or even a deliberate pocket of empty space can reset the eye. Rhythm matters more than minimalism.

This is especially important on mobile. Desktop density can rely on multiple columns and peripheral context. Mobile density has to sequence attention. The interface still needs to feel rich, but it cannot demand simultaneous reading from every part of the screen.

That is why I prefer editorial density over dashboard density for a personal site. Editorial density assumes the reader is moving through meaning. Dashboard density assumes the reader is monitoring state. They are not the same job.

When the goal is writing, the design should be ambitious enough to feel authored and quiet enough to disappear once the reader starts reading. That balance is harder than flamboyant minimalism, but it ages much better.

title: Why Markdown beats a CMS at the beginning
description: A CMS becomes useful when publishing volume justifies it. Before that point, a simple Markdown workflow is usually faster, cheaper, and more durable.
excerpt: When people say they want a “real blog,” they often mean they want a CMS. What they usually need is a stable publishing loop. Those are not the same thing. A CMS is useful when you…
body:
When people say they want a “real blog,” they often mean they want a CMS. What they usually need is a stable publishing loop.

Those are not the same thing.

A CMS is useful when you have multiple editors, a review process, structured content dependencies, or a strong need for non-technical publishing. None of those conditions apply to most personal sites. A personal blog usually has one author, a small number of content types, and a strong need for portability.

That is why I start with Markdown.

Markdown has a few advantages that matter immediately:

- The writing stays readable in raw form.
- Version control becomes automatic.
- Moving between frameworks is dramatically easier.
- The content model stays honest because you can see it directly.

There is also a psychological advantage. Markdown keeps the publishing act close to the writing act. There are fewer panels, fewer configuration detours, and fewer decisions that pretend to be productive. You write, commit, preview, publish.

This does not mean CMS tools are bad. It means they solve a later problem. They become worth the complexity when the bottleneck shifts from authoring to coordination. If the bottleneck is still “I do not publish consistently,” then adding a CMS often creates the wrong kind of sophistication.

The rule I like is simple: choose the smallest system that makes publishing feel inevitable. For a single-author blog, Markdown wins that argument more often than people admit.

When the constraints change, you can migrate. That option is exactly why starting with portable files is such a good default.

title: Tools should remove drag, not add theater
description: Good tooling makes the important path shorter. Bad tooling creates a feeling of sophistication while quietly multiplying friction.
excerpt: There is a kind of tool that looks impressive in demos and feels exhausting in daily use. It usually has one or more of these symptoms: too many states, too many surface-level opti…
body:
There is a kind of tool that looks impressive in demos and feels exhausting in daily use.

It usually has one or more of these symptoms: too many states, too many surface-level options, too much ceremony before you can do obvious work, and a persistent need to explain itself. The problem is not complexity by itself. Some tasks are genuinely complex. The problem is performative complexity.

I care about tools that reduce drag in the path I actually repeat.

For a writing system, that means:

- opening a draft quickly
- previewing it without waiting
- publishing it without hunting through settings
- trusting that the output will remain stable

For a frontend system, it means something similar:

- components are easy to find
- styles are consistent without becoming rigid
- build steps are boring
- debugging feels local instead of mystical

The reason I keep returning to simpler stacks is not nostalgia. It is throughput. When the tool gets out of the way, your standards can go up because your energy is not being spent on infrastructure theater.

That is also why I think personal websites deserve engineering restraint. You do not need enterprise machinery to publish a thoughtful essay. You need a setup that does not punish you for wanting to publish one more paragraph today.

The strongest compliment I can pay a tool is that it lets me stop thinking about the tool. Everything else is secondary.
